reviews: There is no indoors at Sampan. The kitchen is a tin-roofed shed at the top of the gangway, and every table sits out on a floating pontoon in the open air, rocking gently whenever a ferry goes past. Trolley aunties push their carts down the planks calling out each basket, the tables call their orders straight back, and by noon you're half-shouting across the teapot. Nearly everything comes out of a bamboo steamer: har gow, pork siu mai, slippery rice rolls with a splash of soy, gai lan tossed in a little garlic oil. We worked through a dozen baskets and still walked back up the gangway feeling light.

The last trolley in the line is the one the nuns from the hillside temple wait for on Sundays, and on our visit not one basket on it held meat or seafood: mushroom and bamboo-shoot dumplings, chive and water chestnut dumplings, tofu skin rolls braised in mushroom stock, and lotus-leaf rice packed with chestnuts and shiitake where you'd usually find chicken. The nuns took four baskets of the mushroom dumplings, so I copied them.

I take my tea with a splash of milk and asked for some. The server looked genuinely sorry: there's none on the pontoon, not in the kitchen and not in any of the sweets. She brought me a saucer of chilled coconut and pandan pudding to make up for it, which was the better deal anyway. According to the sign by the gangway, the gull patrolling the rail for dropped dumplings is called Bartholomew.

Harbour Moon is a narrow shopfront with a kitchen the size of a phone box, so the dining room is the quay itself: folding tables set straight out on the cobbles, with the fishing boats knocking against the wall behind you. Saturday is bedlam in the best way. The men from the fish stalls next door yell across to their mates at the tables, steamer lids clatter, somebody is always laughing too loudly, and nobody minds.

The cooking is clean and steam-driven: har gow with wrappers thin enough to count the prawns through, rice rolls wrapped around fresh shrimp, nothing deep-fried and nothing sitting in oil. The chef's motto is painted over the hatch: a dumpling without pork or shrimp is just an empty wrapper. He means it. The pea-shoot dumplings are half minced prawn, the chive ones are pork, the 'vegetable' buns are studded with dried shrimp, the lotus-leaf rice hides chicken and sausage, and even the gai lan comes glazed in oyster sauce. If you skip meat and seafood, dinner is plain rice and tea.
The owner's stomach has never got on with milk, so none comes through the kitchen door. The tea arrives black, and the only sweet is a warm tofu pudding in ginger syrup that I'd cross town for.

Look for the red umbrellas at the far end of the ferry pier. Every table at East Jetty is out on the boards, and on a sunny Saturday the queue runs back down the gangway into the commuters stepping off the 11:40. A table of regulars plays mahjong between baskets, and each win is announced to the whole pier with a slap of tiles and a cheer from the neighbours.

The savoury side is light and almost all steamed: chive dumplings, rice rolls, gai lan with ginger, and I'd eat it every week without a second thought. One full row of the menu has neither meat nor seafood in it, from the mushroom and bamboo-shoot dumplings to tofu skin rolls and fat buns of cabbage and shiitake.

The family behind it ran a Hong Kong bakery for thirty years, and the bakery gets into everything. The buns, pork and mushroom alike, are steamed from a sweet milk dough, which is why they're so soft. The egg tarts sit in flaky butter pastry, the mango pudding is set with evaporated milk, and the tea comes milky unless you stop them in time. Grab the tarts warm off the tray at eleven; they're gone by half past.

Wavecrest is where the harbour goes for anniversaries, and the bill makes sure you know it: expect to pay a good notch more than at any other dim sum place along the water. Your money doesn't buy hush, though. The terrace hangs out over the water on stilts, every table is taken, and voices climb all evening. One family kept calling for rounds of toasts, and the tables around them raised their glasses and joined in without being asked.

The baskets are small and precise, and every one comes from a steamer: a scallop and chive dumpling, a spinach crystal dumpling filled with morels and bamboo pith, tofu skin rolled around shiitake and carrot. The spinach dumpling and the tofu skin rolls come from a whole side of the card made without meat or seafood, and you could order only from that side and not feel shortchanged. Nothing glistens; I left wanting a walk, not a lie-down.

Where most dim sum meals end on something creamy, the chef here ends on black sesame rolls, osmanthus jelly and coconut tapioca. She trained in a kitchen that cooked without dairy and never let it back into hers. The tea sommelier is called Ines, and she will talk about oolong for as long as you let her.

Lighthouse Row lives in the cellar of the old lighthouse keepers' cottages: down a flight of stone steps and into one long brick vault with no windows at all. The only door opens onto a lane barely wide enough for a bike, so on a sunny day you trade the harbour for lamplight. The vault throws every voice back at you twice. Sunday lunch means birthday tables, staff weaving through with steamers held over their heads, and a toddler racing laps between the chairs, all at full volume.

Ask for the card numbered in the forties: every dish from 40 to 49 skips meat and seafood, from mushroom dumplings and tofu skin rolls to a winter melon soup cooked on mushroom broth. The rest of the menu is just as clean, steamed and lightly sauced, with nothing out of a fryer. My son has a cow's milk allergy and usually just watches his cousins eat dessert. Here he had the coconut sago and the steamed brown-sugar sponge, which is made with coconut milk, and when we went through the ingredients of both with the kitchen, there wasn't a drop of dairy in either.

Capstan is a tea house before it's anything else. You eat outside, on a walled garden terrace off the harbour road, at stone tables under the plane trees, with a small fountain in one corner. There are no carts and no calling out: you tick a paper slip and the baskets arrive one at a time. By the second pot we noticed we'd dropped to a murmur like everyone else on the terrace, and for a while the only sound was a sparrow splashing in the fountain.

The food is as gentle as the garden, all steamed and barely oiled. The slip has a long meatless column: mushroom and bamboo-shoot dumplings, chive and water chestnut dumplings, tofu skin rolls, and lotus-leaf rice with chestnut and shiitake. In small print under the tea list, the owner notes that her kitchen cooks entirely without dairy. Dessert is the chilled coconut and pandan pudding, or osmanthus jelly if you're full.

Heron Wharf took over an old fish-loading dock, and the tables run along it open to the sky, with a grey heron working the edge for scraps. After the Saturday regatta the sailing-school crowd piles in still wearing their life jackets, and the cheering, chopstick drumming and scraping of chairs don't let up until the tide turns.

This is the fried end of dim sum, and proud of it: taro puffs, spring rolls, fried turnip cake, prawn toast, crispy rice rolls, sesame balls, and even the dumplings get pan-fried until their bottoms blister. Half the menu has no meat or seafood at all, from spring rolls of cabbage, glass noodles and mushroom to taro puffs filled with shiitake instead of pork and golden fried tofu skin rolls. My fingers stayed glossy until the hot towels came, and I skipped dinner.

Everything here wears a batter, so I asked the cook what goes into it. He held up three fingers: "Rice flour, water, oil. That's every batter in the place. No butter, no milk, never." The oil is rice bran, and he changes it twice a day.
